title: What Is Included in a Furnace Inspection?
h1: What Is Included in a Furnace Inspection?
description: A furnace inspection covers safety checks, burners, ignition, venting, the heat exchanger, airflow and controls. Here's what a technician checks and why.
quick_answer: A furnace inspection covers safety and performance. A technician checks the burners, ignition system and flame sensor, inspects the heat exchanger and venting, tests for carbon monoxide, checks gas pressure and safety switches, cleans or checks the blower, measures airflow and temperature rise, inspects electrical connections and the filter, and confirms the thermostat controls the system correctly.
body:
A good furnace inspection does two jobs: it makes sure the furnace is safe to run, and it makes sure the furnace heats your home efficiently. In San Diego and Orange County, furnaces may sit idle for months, then run hard on cold inland nights. That on-and-off pattern is exactly why a check before heating season pays off.

What safety checks are part of the inspection?

Safety comes first with any gas furnace. A technician should:

  • Inspect the heat exchanger for cracks, rust or signs of overheating. A cracked heat exchanger can let combustion gases into your air.
  • Check the venting to make sure exhaust gases leave the house. That means looking at the flue pipe, connections and draft, and checking for blockages.
  • Test for carbon monoxide around the furnace and in the supply air.
  • Check for gas leaks at the gas valve and connections.
  • Test the safety controls, including the high-limit switch, rollout switches and pressure switch, which shut the furnace down if something goes wrong.

If your carbon monoxide alarm ever sounds, get everyone outside and call 911. If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside. Don't try to inspect or repair gas parts yourself.

What parts of the furnace get checked?

  1. Burners: checked for clean, even flames and cleaned if dirty or rusty.
  2. Ignition system: the hot surface igniter or spark igniter is tested for wear.
  3. Flame sensor: cleaned and checked, since a dirty sensor is a very common reason furnaces start and then shut off.
  4. Gas pressure: measured and adjusted to the manufacturer's specs.
  5. Blower: the motor, wheel and capacitor are checked, and the wheel is inspected for dust buildup.
  6. Inducer motor: checked for noise and proper operation on newer furnaces.
  7. Electrical connections: tightened and checked for signs of heat damage.
  8. Condensate drain: on high-efficiency furnaces, cleared so water doesn't back up.

How does a technician check performance?

Once everything looks right, the furnace is run through a full cycle. The technician watches the startup sequence, measures the temperature rise across the furnace to confirm proper airflow, checks the filter and looks at how evenly the heat reaches the rooms.

The thermostat is checked too. It should call for heat when it should, shut off on time and be set up correctly for your system. A poorly placed thermostat, like one in a sunny hallway, can cause short cycling and uneven heating.

Why do Southern California furnaces need inspections?

Mild winters mean furnaces here run less than in colder places, but that doesn't mean they need less attention. Long idle periods let dust settle on burners and flame sensors. Furnaces in attics deal with heat, dust and sometimes rodents. Units in garages pick up dust, and coastal air can corrode metal parts over time.

Many homes also have the furnace in a hall closet near bedrooms, which makes venting and carbon monoxide checks even more important. And when the first cold snap hits, everyone turns on the heat at once, so finding a problem in early fall beats waiting.

What happens if the technician finds a problem?

Small issues, like a dirty flame sensor or a loose wire, are usually handled on the spot. Bigger findings should come with a clear explanation and photos where possible. If there's a safety concern, such as a cracked heat exchanger or a venting problem, the technician may recommend shutting the furnace off until it's repaired. That can feel inconvenient, but it's the right call when combustion gases are involved.

How often should a furnace be inspected?

Once a year is a good rule, ideally in the fall before you need heat. If you have a heat pump, it runs in both summer and winter, so a check in spring and fall makes sense. Our heating service includes full furnace inspections and tune-ups.

What can you do between inspections?

  • Change the filter on schedule, and more often during smoky or dusty stretches
  • Keep the area around the furnace clear of storage, paint and cleaning products
  • Test your carbon monoxide and smoke alarms
  • Listen for new noises and watch for short cycling or a burning smell
  • Make sure returns and registers aren't blocked by furniture
faqs: How long does a furnace inspection take?
Most inspections take about an hour, sometimes longer if the furnace needs cleaning or a part needs attention. Attic furnaces can take a bit more time because of access.
Is a furnace inspection the same as a tune-up?
They overlap. An inspection checks safety and condition, while a tune-up adds cleaning and adjustments, like cleaning the flame sensor and burners. Most service visits include both.
Can a furnace inspection find carbon monoxide problems?
Yes. Technicians check the heat exchanger and venting and test for carbon monoxide. That's one of the main reasons for a yearly inspection. You should still keep working CO alarms in the home.
Do I need a furnace inspection if I barely use my heat?
Yes. Furnaces that sit idle collect dust on burners and sensors, and safety parts like the venting and heat exchanger still need checking before the first cold night.
